method: rMSSD is the root mean square of successive differences between R-R intervals, a time-domain heart-rate-variability measure that consumer wearables commonly report for an overnight or morning reading; this page works in milliseconds. The baseline is the arithmetic mean of the most recent 7, 14 or 28 readings you paste, and the spread is the sample standard deviation with n minus 1 in the denominator, sqrt(sum of squared deviations / (n - 1)). The coefficient of variation is the standard deviation divided by the mean, times 100, so variability can be compared between windows whose absolute rMSSD differs. The z-score is (latest reading - baseline mean) / standard deviation: it is labelled inside one standard deviation when |z| < 1, outside one standard deviation when 1 <= |z| < 2, and two or more standard deviations otherwise, always with the direction shown, and it is not computed at all when every reading in the window is identical. The trend is an ordinary least-squares slope of reading against position in the window, reported in milliseconds per reading; it describes the past window and is not a forecast. The chart plots at most the last 28 readings with the baseline mean and the mean plus or minus one standard deviation band. Readings are limited to 3 to 180 values of 5 to 300 ms, and the window is limited to 7, 14 or 28 readings; when fewer readings are available than the window asks for, every available reading is used and the page says so. The page reports descriptive statistics for the user's own numbers only: it makes no diagnosis, produces no readiness score, gives no training or medical advice, and does not account for device, sensor, posture or measurement-time differences. Everything is computed in the browser with no uploads, network access or storage.
